query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The formation and crystal‐structure selection in noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles are determined by a kinetic trapping mechanism: rapid heating homogenizes the elemental distribution and forms a metastable amorphous precursor, and ultrafast quenching kinetically freezes this configuration into a single-phase solid solution. However, when the cooling rate is reduced even slightly, increased atomic mobility allows for local atomic rearrangements that lead to phase separation, elemental segregation, and the formation of undesired secondary crystalline phases.
generation.material_initial_state: Noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles synthesized under rapid heating and quenching conditions aimed at achieving a single-phase solid-solution.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the cooling rate during synthesis while keeping the overall composition and heating rate constant (i.e., adjust the thermal quenching profile).
generation.conditions: Synthesis of multi-element noble metal nanoparticles using rapid heating (to achieve melting and homogenization) followed by controlled cooling rates; the study should be conducted near the melting point of the alloy components where atomic diffusion is significant.
generation.structural_mediator: A transient metastable amorphous phase that forms during rapid heating and whose atomic configuration determines the nucleation pathway under kinetic constraints.
generation.mechanism: The competitive interplay of rapid energy input (that forces homogeneous mixing) and the quench rate (which either traps the high-entropy configuration or allows enough atomic diffusion for segregation) governs the final crystal structure. Extremely rapid quenching preserves the single-phase state by freezing the amorphous precursor, while even slightly slower quenching permits atomic rearrangements that drive phase separation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under ultrafast cooling conditions, nanoparticles retain a uniform single-phase solid solution. If the cooling rate is moderately reduced, one will observe increased phase separation, elemental segregation, and deviations in particle morphology and crystal structure relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced under standard rapid heating with ultrafast quenching that maintain a uniform, single-phase HEA structure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies when the synthesis is conducted in regimes where the heating is sufficiently rapid to homogenize the multi-element composition and where the cooling rate is near a critical threshold that determines whether the amorphous precursor is kinetically trapped or allowed to relax into multiple phases. Outside of these regimes (e.g., extremely slow cooling or excessive overheating), thermodynamic factors may dominate the phase selection.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical cooling rate and the quantitative balance between diffusion rates and quenching kinetics are uncertain because of the complex interplay of nanoscale processes and elemental diffusion barriers. Further systematic experiments are needed to determine these thresholds.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles under identical rapid heating conditions but vary only the cooling (quenching) rate. Use in situ thermal monitoring to precisely control and record the cooling profiles.
measurements: Cooling rate profiles recorded during synthesis
Phase composition and crystallinity using X-ray diffraction (XRD)
Elemental distribution and segregation via high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles synthesized with moderately slower cooling rates do not show a significant transition from a uniform single-phase structure to mixed phases (i.e., no detectable increase in phase separation or segregation compared to those synthesized under ultra-rapid quench conditions), then the proposed kinetic trapping mechanism hypothesis is falsified.

Design and Development of High-Entropy Alloys with a Tailored Composition and Phase Structure Based on Thermodynamic Parameters and Film Thickness Using a Novel Combinatorial Target

Abstract: This study presents a novel synthesis route for high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and high-entropy metallic glass (HEMG) using radio frequency (RF) magnetron sputtering and controlling the HEA phase selection according to atomic size difference (δ) and film thickness. The preparation of HEAs using sputtering requires either multitargets or the preparation of a target containing at least five distinct elements. In developing HEA-preparation techniques, the emergence of a novel sputtering target system is promising to prepare a wide range of HEAs. High-Entropy Oxides in the Mullite-Type Structure

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy materials (HEMs) represent a new class of solid solutions containing at least five different elements. Their compositional diversity makes them promising as platforms for the development of functional materials. We synthesized new HEMs in a mullite-type structure and present five compounds, i.e., Bi2(Al0.25Ga0.25Fe0.25Mn0.25)4O9 and A2Mn4O10 with variations of A = Nd, Sm, Y, Er, Eu, Ce, and Bi, demonstrating the vast accessible composition space. By combining scattering, microscopy, and spectroscopy techniques, we show that our materials are mixed solid solutions. Remarkably, when following their crystallization in situ using X-ray diffraction and X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we find that the HEMs form through a metastable amorphous phase without the formation of any crystalline intermediates. We expect that our synthesis is excellently suited to synthesizing diverse HEMs and therefore will have a significant impact on their future exploration.

Synthesis and Unique Behaviors of High-Purity HEA Nanoparticles Using Femtosecond Laser Ablation

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) are a class of metal alloys consisting of four or more molar equal or near-equal elements. HEA nanomaterials have garnered significant interest due to their wide range of applications, such as electrocatalysis, welding, and brazing. Their unique multi-principle high-entropy effect allows for the tailoring of the alloy composition to facilitate specific electrochemical reactions. This study focuses on the synthesis of high-purity HEA nanoparticles using the method of femtosecond laser ablation synthesis in liquid. The use of ultrashort energy pulses in femtosecond lasers enables uniform ablation of materials at significantly lower power levels compared to longer pulse or continuous pulse lasers. We investigate how various femtosecond laser parameters affect the morphology, phase, and other characteristics of the synthesized nanoparticles. An innovative aspect of our solution is its ability to rapidly generate multi-component nanoparticles with a high fidelity as the input multi-component target material at a significant yielding rate. A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.
